questions.problem:
Express ${\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[3($
{{field-1}}
$)^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=3{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[3{(\,1+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[5{(2+\frac{4k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

$$
f(x)=5{x}^{3}\,\text{and}\,b=6.

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{3k}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\displaystyle \int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = 4-x,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{3-1}{n} = \dfrac 2 n,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(4-x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{2}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(4-(1+\frac{2k}{n}))\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(3-\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral
canonical_examples.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $\displaystyle \int_{3}^b f(x)\, \textrm d x =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
\int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f\left(x_k\right)\cdot \Delta x
$$

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a = 3.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $\Delta x = \dfrac{5}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\dfrac{5}{n} = \dfrac{b-3}{n} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad b = 8.
$$

Consequently, $x_k = 3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}$ and $f(x_k) = x_{k}^2.$

Hence,

$$
\int_{3}^{8} x^2 \, \textrm d x =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)= x^2$ and $b = 8.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x$ as the limit of a right Riemann sum.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k)\cdot\Delta x,
$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x =  \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = x^2,$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{2-1}{n} = \dfrac 1 n.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{k}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{(1+\frac{k}{n})}^{2}\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we want to approximate the area $\mathcal A$ bound by the curve $y= x^2+1$ and the lines $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14223546/assets/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14223546/assets/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(0+k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({(k\cdot Δx)}^{2}+1)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({k}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}(\frac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the above, we used the fact that $x_k = 0 + k\Delta x = k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{1 - 0}{n} = \dfrac 1 n,$ as we've seen before.

The exact area is found by computing the limit as $n\to\infty.$ So instead of using an approximation symbol $(\approx),$ we can now use an equality symbol and write

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.
$$

The formula above is a bit clunky, so instead of writing it using limits and sigma notation, we introduce a new notation called the **definite integral**, defined as

$$
\mathcal{A} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}= \int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our example, 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1 (x^2+1)\, \textrm{d}x
$$

can be interpreted as the exact area under the graph of $y = f(x) = x^2+1$ between $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis.

tutorials.name: General Notation
tutorials.problem:
In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

The limit $x=a$ is referred to as the **lower limit**, whereas $x=b$ is called the **upper limit**.
tutorials.title: General Notation
tutorials.content:
In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

The limit $x=a$ is referred to as the **lower limit**, whereas $x=b$ is called the **upper limit**.

tutorials.name: Using a Right Riemann Sum
tutorials.problem:
There's nothing special about using a left Riemann sum to define a definite integral. A definite integral can also be defined as the limit of a right Riemann sum,

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,\textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k)\cdot\Delta x,
$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x =  \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

Nothing has changed, except that the index starts from $k=1$ instead of $k=0$, and goes up to $k=n.$ 

**Note:** In the limit as $n \to \infty,$ the left and right Riemann sums give *the exact same result*!
